text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer, in a veiled attack on Britain, slammed on Wednesday countries he said wanted the EU to bring in new members but were blocking the method of achieving it.

In a speech to the European Parliament, Santer said it was "incompatible" for countries to argue for a huge enlargement into central and eastern Europe and at the same time to fight against changing the EU's institutions.

"Those who are most firmly against institutional reform are the keenest supporters of enlargement," he said. "(But) those who oppose reforms are inevitably slowing the acceptance of the first new members."

Britain, whose ruling government is almost at civil war over Europe, is keen to see the Union's market expand but is vehemently opposed to many of the reforms others in the 15-nation bloc are seeking.
Most notably this includes the right of countries to veto EU policies they do not like. Others argue that with 10 or more new members the EU will have to take more decisions by majority vote.
Santer, who has been turning up the heat recently on Britain, also said that Euro-sceptic arguments that "Brussels" was out to destroy national soveriegnty were false.
"'Brussels' is the member states meeting together," he said. "Providing the means to give strength to national interests globally...is safeguarding national sovereignty.
"No member state is capable of acting alone. Those who believe we can slip back to old ideas, such as a (simple) free trade zone, have a peculiar view of the realities of the world," he said.

"The European Union is not the enemy of national sovereignty. On the contrary, those who want to strengthen sovereignty in the world of today and tomorrow can only do it with a strong and influential Union," Santer said.
